answer.label: Not Terry Pratchett — an anonymous quip
answer.authorDates: compact quip circulating by 1991; pinned firmly on Pratchett by 2004
answer.sourceLine: No book, article or interview by Terry Pratchett is known to contain this line. Quote Investigator ↗ finds the short quip circulating anonymously by 1991. Pratchett’s name was only guessed at in 1998 and 2002, and the earliest unequivocal ascription to him that QI found is in the 2004 quotation book The Guide to Laughing at Family. The idea itself is older: Violet Hunt had it in 1905 and P. G. Wodehouse in 1933.

source.excerpt: In ancient times cats were worshipped as gods; they have not forgotten this.
trail: 1905: in Violet Hunt’s The Cat, narrated by a cat, the mother cat teaches that cats go back “to the days beyond the dawn of history, when cats were worshipped” and that “we must never forget that great fact” (p. 51, Internet Archive ↗).
1933: P. G. Wodehouse’s Mulliner Nights says that cats “have never completely got over the snootiness caused by the fact that in Ancient Egypt they were worshipped as gods” (Internet Archive ↗).

1991–2004: the compact quip shows up anonymously on Usenet (1991), in a Hallmark book (1992) and in newspapers (1998). Usenet posters guess at Pratchett in 1998 and 2002, and a 2004 quotation book is the first to credit him without reservation, per Quote Investigator ↗.

Wikiquote lists the line on its Terry Pratchett page ↗ but cites only later books that quote it (2007, 2009). A 2022 note on its talk page ↗ reports that it could not be found in The Unadulterated Cat or Pyramids and asks for a primary source.
source.excerptNote: This is the modern wording as it appears in Quote Investigator’s chronology for 2004. Older forms say “Thousands of years ago” or “The Egyptians worshipped cats” and end with “never forgotten.” Wikiquote spells it “worshiped.”

source.rightsNote: This exact wording has no known author. It surfaces anonymously in the 1990s and is credited to Pratchett without a source, so there is no work or author whose copyright status could honestly be stated. The older passages by Violet Hunt (1905) and P. G. Wodehouse (1933) are different sentences, not the source of this line.

author.name: Terry Pratchett
author.heading: Terry Pratchett — credited, not the author
author.metaLine: 1948–2015 · English fantasy author and satirist, creator of Discworld
author.bio: Sir Terry Pratchett was an English author, humorist and satirist, best known for the Discworld series of 41 comic fantasy novels (1983–2015) and for Good Omens (1990), which he co-wrote with Neil Gaiman. He really did write sharp jokes about cats, in Lords and Ladies and The Amazing Maurice and His Educated Rodents for example. That made him a believable home for a stray cat quip, but the evidence does not show that he wrote this one.

misattribution.heading: How Terry Pratchett got the credit
misattribution.intro: A cat joke with no known author drifted onto a writer known for cat jokes. The record shows the quip in anonymous circulation for years before anyone put Pratchett’s name on it, and even then only as a guess at first.

items.why: Pratchett’s name first comes up as a guess in Usenet threads (“It sounds Pratchett-ish?” in 1998, “Terry Pratchett, iirc” in 2002). The earliest unequivocal ascription is a 2004 quotation book, and QI has found “no substantive evidence” that he created the joke, per Quote Investigator ↗.

items.who: Dusty Rainbolt and other cat books
items.why: Wikiquote’s only citations for the Pratchett credit are Ghost Cats (2007) by Dusty Rainbolt and a 2009 Chicken Soup for the Soul volume. Both are books quoting the line, not Pratchett’s own writing (Wikiquote ↗).

In 1933 Wodehouse wrote that cats “have never completely got over the snootiness caused by the fact that in Ancient Egypt they were worshipped as gods” (Mulliner Nights ↗). It is the same joke, but not this wording.

items.scope: Earliest known version of the idea
items.why: Her cat narrator is taught that cats go back to the days “when cats were worshipped” and that “we must never forget that great fact.” QI calls this the earliest match (The Cat, p. 51 ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is anonymous. Quote Investigator traces the idea to Violet Hunt (1905) and Wodehouse (1933) and the compact quip to anonymous use by 1991, and suggests the Pratchett credit came about in two steps: a tentative guess first, then a firm ascription by 2004 (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Pratchett
lead: Pratchett wrote plenty of real cat humor. In Lords and Ladies a character says that “if cats looked like frogs we’d realise what nasty, cruel little bastards they are,” and the narrator of The Amazing Maurice and His Educated Rodents observes that cats “know” they are lords of creation. Quote Investigator suggests lines like these probably made the misattribution easy to believe.

The pattern is a familiar one. Usenet posters half-remembered the line as “Pratchett-ish,” a quotation book then printed his name without hedging, and calendars, cat anthologies and even a 2011 Pratchett biography repeated it with no citation.
context.pull: QI has found no substantive evidence that Terry Pratchett created this joke.
